What can be said: seafarers sought the Great Gods, and Apollonius parks Jason's crew in that queue.

primarySources.text: They reached Electra's isle, where they were initiated in the sacred rites, that they might sail with greater safety.

name: Cyzicus
description: The city of the Doliones on the Propontis, where in Argonautica Book 1 the Argonauts, blown back by night, fought their former hosts unrecognised and killed the young king Cyzicus.
detailedBio:
## Night battle with friends

In *Argonautica* 1 the Argonauts are hosted by Cyzicus, young king of the Doliones. They leave, are blown back in the dark, and kill him by mistake. His bride Cleite hangs herself; the people bury him. It is a tragic layover in the Propontis, not a monster fight. The city of Cyzicus was real. Apollonius is the narrative source. There is no major independent Cyzicus epic. The stop costs an ally to weather and misrecognition.

primarySources.text: They did not know they had returned to the Doliones. In the night they slew Cyzicus, their host.

name: Land of the Bebryces
description: The Bithynian land of the Bebryces, whose king Amycus forced strangers to box with him until Polydeuces defeated him for the Argonauts (Argonautica 2; Theocritus, Idyll 22).
detailedBio:
## Amycus at the shore

*Argonautica* 2: the Bebryces' king Amycus forces strangers to box and kills them. Polydeuces (Pollux) takes the challenge, breaks him, and the Argonauts scatter the Bebryces. The land is a Bithynian shore. Theocritus *Idyll* 22 tells the same bout. There is no Bebrycian cult in Greece. The stop is a ritual of hostile hospitality solved with fists, a Dioscuric set-piece before the clashing rocks.

primarySources.text: Amycus came down and said: Stranger, it is the law that no man leave until he has lifted his hands against me.

name: Symplegades (Clashing Rocks)
description: The Clashing Rocks at the entrance to the Black Sea, which crushed anything passing between them until the Argo, following Phineus's advice and a dove, slipped through and fixed them in place.
detailedBio:
## Clashing rocks at the Bosporus

The Symplegades (Planctae in some naming muddles) are living cliffs that smash what passes. In *Argonautica* 2 Phineus tells the crew to send a dove; if it lives, row. Athena shoves the Argo through; the rocks freeze apart thereafter. Pindar already knows the feat. There is no cult of the rocks. Later sailors pointed at the Bosporus. The episode is a one-time opening of the Black Sea.

primarySources.text: They let fly the dove. The rocks sheared her tail-feathers, then they drove the Argo through, and the rocks stood still thereafter.

name: Libyan Desert Shore
description: The desert coast of North Africa where, in Argonautica Book 4, the Argonauts were stranded in the shallows of the Syrtis and carried the Argo overland for twelve days before Triton showed them the sea.
detailedBio:
## The Argo on sand

*Argonautica* 4 strands the crew on a Libyan syrtis. They portage the Argo inland for days, meet the Hesperides after Heracles has already taken the apples, and lose companions to snake and exhaustion. Triton finally shows the sea-road. This is not Odysseus's lotus shore. Apollonius is expanding a North African detour. There is no Libyan Argonaut cult. The desert is a second labor of carrying a ship where water should have been.

primarySources.text: They lifted the Argo on their shoulders and bore her across the Libyan sands, toward the Tritonian mere.

name: Nidavellir
description: Niðavellir, 'dark fields', named in the Völuspá as a place of the dwarves and a hall of gold; modern retellings often treat it as the dwarves' forge-realm and equate it with Svartalfheim.
detailedBio:
## Dwarf-fields, overlapping Svartalfheim

*Voluspa* mentions Niðavellir, "dark fields," as a dwarf-place (and a hall of gold). Snorri prefers Svartalfheim for underground smiths. English Nidavellir is a modern convenience for the same workshop: Draupnir, Mjolnir, Gleipnir's makers. There is no separate cult. Admit the overlap rather than invent two kingdoms with flags. The poems need a dark address for skilled beings who are not Aesir.

primarySources.text: Stood in the north, on Nidavellir, a hall of gold, the dwelling of Sindri's kin.

name: Western Horizon
description: The akhet of the west, where the sun god sets each evening to enter the Duat, and the direction of the dead, whom Egyptian texts call 'westerners' under the rule of Osiris.
detailedBio:
## Akhet of the setting sun

The western horizon (akhet) is where Ra enters the Duat each evening and where the dead are "westerners" under Osiris. Pyramid Texts and later underworld books orient tombs and spells toward that descent. It is a daily cosmological door, not a city. Abydos and the necropolis edges of Thebes are earthly analogues. There is no single gatehouse excavated as "the" horizon. The west is a direction of completion and danger.

primarySources.text: The king goes to the western horizon, among the followers of Re, among the imperishable stars.

name: First Gate of the Duat
description: The first of the gates the sun god's night barque passes in the New Kingdom underworld books such as the Book of Gates, each guarded by serpents and doorkeepers whose names must be known.
detailedBio:
## Password at hour one

New Kingdom underworld books (*Book of Gates*, *Amduat*) divide the night into gates and hours. The first gate is where the sun-barque and the deceased must know names to pass. Tomb walls in the Valley of the Kings draw the doorkeepers. There is no civic cult of "First Gate." It is liturgical architecture for a royal night-journey. Later *Book of the Dead* spells keep the same anxiety: speak, or be turned back.

primarySources.text: The first gate of the West: the name of its keeper is spoken, and the barque of Re enters the darkness.
primarySources.source: Book of Gates / Amduat, First Hour–Gate

name: Hall of Ma'at
description: The Hall of the Two Truths, where the heart of the dead is weighed against the feather of Maat before Osiris and forty-two judges, as described in Book of the Dead Spell 125.
detailedBio:
## Weighing of the heart

The Hall of Two Truths (Maat) is where the deceased's heart is weighed against the feather, Anubis adjusting the scale, Thoth recording, Ammit waiting. *Book of the Dead* Spell 125 is the great negative confession before forty-two judges. Osiris presides. This is the moral bottleneck of the Egyptian afterlife as New Kingdom officials imagined it. There is no separate temple of the Hall; coffins and papyri are the building.

primarySources.text: I have not done falsehood against men. I have not impoverished my fellows. My heart is weighed in the Hall of Maat.

name: Lake of Fire
description: A lake of flame in the Egyptian underworld books and Book of the Dead, which destroys the enemies of the sun god and the unjust dead while refreshing the justified.
detailedBio:
## A lake that unmakes the unjust

The Lake of Fire appears in *Book of the Dead* vignettes and in underworld books as a place that destroys enemies of Re and the unjust dead, while the justified may drink. It is not Dante. Ammit and knife-wielding demons work nearby. There is no excavated crater. The image is a warning painted beside the successful farmer in Aaru: the same cosmos has a disposal pit for those who fail the names and the scale.

primarySources.text: The Lake of Fire: the unjust are fallen into it, but the justified live on the offerings of Re.
primarySources.source: Book of the Dead (fire-lake vignettes) / Amduat

name: Throne of Osiris
description: The throne of Osiris as king of the dead and ruler of the West, the goal of the justified dead in the Egyptian afterlife texts, and in cult associated above all with Abydos.
detailedBio:
## The western king

Osiris sits as king of the dead, often at Abydos in cult and in the Hall of Judgment in books of the afterlife. Pyramid Texts already identify the dead king with Osiris. Later the throne is the end of the justified path: green skin, crook and flail, Isis beside him. There is no rival "palace tour" text. The throne is an office. Abydos supplies the earthly house; the Duat supplies the courtroom.

primarySources.text: You are Osiris, and you sit upon the throne of Osiris, at the head of the westerners.

name: Nemea
description: The valley in the northeast Peloponnese where Heracles performed his first labour, strangling the Nemean lion whose hide no weapon could pierce; later the site of the Nemean Games.
detailedBio:
## First labor, uncuttable hide

Apollodorus *Library* 2.5.1: Heracles' first labor for Eurystheus is the Nemean lion, whose skin weapons will not pierce. He traps it in a cave and strangles it, then wears the hide. Nemea in the Argolid later hosted games for Zeus; the lion is not a cult animal there in the labor text. Hesiod and Pindar already know the beast. The place is a valley with a monster that sets the hero's costume.

primarySources.text: He shot the lion, but when he perceived that the beast was invulnerable, he threw away his bow and strangled it with his arms.

name: Lerna
description: The spring-fed marsh near Argos where Heracles and Iolaus killed the many-headed Hydra in the second labour, burning each neck and burying the immortal head under a rock.
detailedBio:
## Hydra in the marsh

Apollodorus 2.5.2: the second labor is the Lernaean Hydra, a many-headed water-snake in the swamp of Lerna, with one immortal head. Iolaus burns the necks; Heracles buries the immortal head under a rock and dips his arrows in the gall. Hera sent a crab; both beast and crab become constellations in later sky-lore. Lerna's springs were real. Mystery-cult gossip about Lerna is separate from this kill.

primarySources.text: He cut off the immortal head and buried it, and put a heavy rock on it, beside the road that leads through Lerna to Elaius.

name: Ceryneia
description: The Arcadian hills of the Ceryneian hind, the golden-horned deer sacred to Artemis that Heracles pursued for a year in his third labour and brought back alive.
detailedBio:
## Hind of Artemis

Apollodorus 2.5.3: the third labor is to bring the Ceryneian hind alive, a golden-horned deer sacred to Artemis. Heracles hunts it a year, wounds it, and argues with Artemis and Apollo before they allow the loan to Eurystheus. The hills are in Achaea. There is no independent hind-epic. The labor is a piety test: catch the goddess's animal without claiming it as meat.

primarySources.text: It was a hind with golden horns, sacred to Artemis. He hunted it a whole year.

name: Mount Erymanthos
description: The Arcadian mountain of the Erymanthian boar, which Heracles drove into deep snow and captured alive in his fourth labour, after a fatal fight with the centaurs on the way.
detailedBio:
## Boar on the mountain, centaurs at dinner

Apollodorus 2.5.4: the fourth labor is the Erymanthian boar, to be brought alive. On the way Heracles dines with Pholus; opened wine draws centaurs, and a fight kills friends (and, in the long run, Chiron). He then drives the boar into snow and nets it. Mount Erymanthos is in Arcadia. The labor is a capture; the centaur episode is the moral mess attached to the mountain.

primarySources.text: He chased the boar from the thicket with shouts, drove it into deep snow, and trapped it in a net.

name: Augean Stables
description: The cattle stables of King Augeas of Elis, uncleaned for years, which Heracles cleared in a single day in his fifth labour by diverting the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through them.
detailedBio:
## A river through a king's filth

Apollodorus 2.5.5: the fifth labor is to clean Augeas's stables in a day. Heracles diverts the Alpheus (and/or Peneus), then is cheated of pay. Later he sacks Elis. Olympia sits in the same region; do not confuse the labor with the games' charter, though some stories try. The stables are a hygiene miracle with a lawsuit attached. There is no surviving cult of the dung-heap.

primarySources.text: He made a breach in the foundation of the cattle-yard and turned in the rivers Alpheus and Peneus, and the water carried the dung out.

name: Lake Stymphalus
description: The Arcadian lake and marsh of the Stymphalian birds, which Heracles startled into flight with a bronze rattle from Athena and shot down in his sixth labour.
detailedBio:
## Birds off the water

Apollodorus 2.5.6: the sixth labor is the Stymphalian birds, man-eating (or at least brazen) waterfowl in an Arcadian marsh. Athena gives a bronze rattle; Heracles flushes them and shoots. The lake is real. There is no bird-goddess cult required by Apollodorus. The labor is a wetland pest-control with a borrowed instrument. Pausanias later saw Stymphalos as a town with a temple of Artemis.

primarySources.text: Athena gave him a bronze rattle. He scared the birds from the wood, and shot them as they flew.

name: Thrace
description: The wild northern land of the Thracians, home of King Diomedes, son of Ares, whose man-eating mares Heracles captured in his eighth labour after feeding the king to them.
detailedBio:
## Diomedes's mares

Apollodorus 2.5.8: the eighth labor takes Heracles to Thrace, to the man-eating mares of King Diomedes, son of Ares. He feeds Diomedes to his own horses (in the usual version), then brings the team to Eurystheus. Thrace in myth is a northern elsewhere: Ares, harsh kings, wild horses. The labor is not a tour of Thracian religion. Euripides' *Alcestis* already assumes Heracles heading toward these mares.

primarySources.text: He killed Diomedes and brought the mares to Eurystheus. They were man-eating.

name: Themiscyra
description: The Amazon city on the river Thermodon on the southern Black Sea coast, where Heracles went in his ninth labour for the war-belt of the Amazon queen Hippolyta.
detailedBio:
## Amazon shore, Hippolyta's belt

Apollodorus 2.5.9: the ninth labor is Hippolyta's girdle, a gift of Ares, at Themiscyra on the Thermodon. The Amazons receive him until Hera starts a rumor; fighting follows; the belt is taken. Herodotus later historicizes Amazons; the labor does not. Themiscyra is a Black Sea address for a female warrior politeia. The girdle is a token, not a city's constitution.

primarySources.text: He was sent to fetch the belt of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, which Ares had given her.

name: Erytheia
description: The red island of the far west, beyond the Ocean, where the three-bodied giant Geryon kept his cattle; Heracles sailed there in the Sun's golden cup for his tenth labour.
detailedBio:
## Geryon's red island

Apollodorus 2.5.10: the tenth labor is the cattle of Geryon, a three-bodied giant on Erytheia in the far west, with the herdsman Eurytion and the dog Orthrus. Heracles crosses in the golden cup of the Sun, kills them, and drives the herd back. Stesichorus's *Geryoneis* is an older poetic witness. Erytheia is a sunset island, later pointed at Gades. There is no Greek colony-cult of Geryon required by the labor.

primarySources.text: He embarked in the cup and sailed to Erytheia. He killed Orthrus and Eurytion, then Geryon, and drove the cattle away.

name: Garden of the Hesperides
description: The garden at the western edge of the world where the Hesperides and the serpent Ladon guarded Hera's golden apples, which Heracles obtained, with or without Atlas's help, in his eleventh labour.
detailedBio:
## Apples at the world's west

Apollodorus 2.5.11: the eleventh labor is the golden apples of the Hesperides, guarded by a dragon (Ladon) in a western garden of Atlas's daughters. Versions split: Heracles holds the sky while Atlas fetches the fruit, or he kills the dragon himself. The garden is not Eden and not a Greek orchard you can visit. It is a sunset horticulture of immortality-adjacent fruit for a goddess (Hera) who did not want it stolen.

primarySources.text: These apples were not in Libya, as some have said, but on Mount Atlas, among the Hyperboreans. The Hesperides guarded them, and the dragon Ladon.

name: Eridu
description: The ancient city in southern Iraq that the Sumerian King List names as the first seat of kingship, home of Enki's temple the E-abzu over the freshwater deep, and one of the oldest settlements in Mesopotamia.
detailedBio:
## First city, Enki's deep

Eridu in the *Sumerian King List* is the first city where kingship descended from heaven. Enki/Ea's temple E-abzu sits on the freshwater deep. Myths (*Enki and the World Order*, *Inanna and Enki*) make it a storehouse of me, the arts of civilization. Archaeology confirms an early sacred precinct on the southern alluvium. It is not Babylon and not Uruk. The claim is priority: water, wisdom, and the first brick platform.

primarySources.text: When kingship was lowered from heaven, kingship was in Eridu.

name: Nippur
description: The holy city of Enlil in central Mesopotamia, whose Ekur temple conferred divine approval on kingship over Sumer and Akkad, and whose scribal schools preserved much of Sumerian literature.
detailedBio:
## Enlil's ratification

Nippur (Nibru) is Enlil's city, the Ekur temple, where kingship of the land is religiously authorized even when political capitals sit elsewhere. Sumerian hymns and the *Sumerian King List* treat it as a cosmic office. It is not a creation battlefield like Babylon in *Enuma Elish*. Archaeology shows a long-lived scribal and temple center. Mythic narrative uses Nippur as the place Enlil's word binds. No hero-quest is required.

primarySources.text: Enlil, whose Ekur in Nippur is the mooring-pole of heaven and earth.

name: Palenque
description: Maya city of Pakal's dynasty — temples of the sun, cross, and inscriptions that map royal myth onto stone.
detailedBio:
## Lakamha, Pakal's inscribed mountain

Palenque (Lakamha) is a Classic Maya city in Chiapas whose Temple of the Inscriptions and Cross Group write K'inich Janaab Pakal's dynasty into stone: descent, maize, the world tree, sun and rain gods. This is not the K'iche' *Popol Vuh*, though the imagery rhymes with later highland myth. The texts are hieroglyphic and royal. The site is a specific court's cosmic autobiography.

primarySources.text: Pakal entered the road of the dead beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions; the tablets name his line and the gods of the Cross Group.
primarySources.source: Palenque Temple of the Inscriptions and Cross Group texts

name: Arkona
description: The temple of Svantevit on Cape Arkona, the northern tip of the island of Rügen, the last great pagan shrine of the Baltic Slavs before its destruction by the Danes in 1168.
detailedBio:
## The last pagan stronghold on the Baltic

Arkona stood on the chalk cliffs at the northern tip of Rügen, fortified by earthen ramparts that still survive as an archaeological site today. It was the principal shrine of the Rani, a West Slavic tribe, and housed the four-faced idol of Svantevit described in detail by the Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus in Book 14 of his *Gesta Danorum*: a wooden temple within the fortress, a great carved image holding a horn and a sword, and a sacred white horse used to divine the outcome of wars.

## Destruction, 1168

Saxo reports that the Danish king Valdemar I, guided by Bishop Absalon of Roskilde, besieged and took Arkona in 1168, forcing the Rani to accept Christianity and surrender the idol, which was reportedly cut apart and burned before the assembled army. The event marks the effective end of organized paganism among the Baltic Slavs and is one of the best-documented single episodes in the whole corpus of Slavic pagan history, precisely because the Danish side had every reason to record its own victory in detail. Archaeological excavation at the site since the 19th century has confirmed the fortress ramparts and settlement layers, though coastal erosion has since destroyed part of the original promontory.

primarySources.text: The city of Arkona [...] stood on a high cliff [...] within its rampart there was a wooden temple, skillfully built, but honored less for its craftsmanship than for the majesty of the god it enshrined.
primarySources.date: composed c. 1200–1216, describing the site destroyed in 1168

name: Starokyivska Hill
description: The hill outside Prince Vladimir's palace in Kiev where, per the Russian Primary Chronicle, six idols — Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh — were raised in 980 and pulled down again in 988.
detailedBio:
## The site of the state pantheon

The *Russian Primary Chronicle* records that in 980, before his conversion, Prince Vladimir of Kiev set up six wooden idols on a hill just outside his palace: Perun given pride of place with a silver head and golden moustache, alongside Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh. This was, as far as the chronicle records, a deliberate act of state religious policy by a newly established prince, drawing together gods from across the peoples he ruled rather than a single inherited local cult site. The hill is generally located in what is now the historic Starokyivska ("Old Kiev") Hill area of the city, near the later Desyatynna Church.

## Dismantled in 988

After Vladimir's baptism and the mass conversion of Kiev in 988, the chronicle reports the same idols being torn down: Perun's image was bound to a horse's tail, dragged down the hill and beaten with sticks, then thrown into the Dnieper and, per the chronicle's account, escorted downstream past the rapids by men posted along the bank to make sure it did not wash ashore and be venerated again. The episode is one of the most vivid and specific passages in the whole chronicle, and is read by historians as much for what it says about Vladimir's political theater of conversion as for what it says about the gods themselves.

primarySources.text: And Vladimir began to reign alone in Kiev, and he set up idols on the hill outside the palace [...] and the people sacrificed to them, calling them gods.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

primarySources.text: And they dragged Perun down to the Dnieper [...] and he ordered men to push it off with poles until it had passed the rapids.
primarySources.date: entry for 988 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

name: Szczecin (Triglav's Temple)
description: The Pomeranian city where Bishop Otto of Bamberg's mission of 1124–1128 destroyed the temple of the three-headed god Triglav, according to the near-contemporary Lives of Otto written by Ebbo and Herbord.
detailedBio:
## A Pomeranian cult center

Szczecin (German Stettin) was a major Pomeranian town and, per the biographers of Bishop Otto of Bamberg, home to a temple of the three-headed god Triglav, along with several other lesser shrines that Otto's mission targeted. Ebbo's *Vita Ottonis* (c. 1151) and Herbord's *Dialogus de Vita Ottonis* (c. 1158) both describe Otto's arrival in 1124–1128, sent at the request of the Polish duke Bolesław III to convert recently subjugated Pomerania, and both give Szczecin's temples the fullest individual treatment of any site in the mission.

## Conversion and demolition

The biographers describe the Szczecin temples being emptied of their treasure and dismantled after negotiation with local elites rather than by force alone, in contrast to the violent Danish conquest of Arkona forty years later. A golden image of Triglav's three heads was reportedly sent to Rome as a gift to Pope Honorius II, framed by the biographers as proof of the mission's success. As with Arkona, the account comes entirely from the converting side, writing to celebrate Otto's later canonization; the temple's internal religious meaning to the Pomeranians themselves is filtered through that lens.

primarySources.text: In the city of Stettin there were four temples [...] but one, the greatest and most splendid, was built with wonderful skill [...] in it stood the triple-headed image called Triglav.
primarySources.source: Herbord, Dialogus de Vita Ottonis episcopi Babenbergensis (paraphrase)

name: Peryn
description: An open-air sanctuary south of Novgorod on the Volkhov river, identified by archaeologists as a likely Perun cult site and named by the First Novgorod Chronicle as the place where his idol was thrown into the river in 989.
detailedBio:
## An excavated open-air site

Peryn sits on the west bank of the Volkhov river, near where it drains from Lake Ilmen, just south of Novgorod. Soviet-era excavations (led by V. V. Sedov in the 1940s–50s) uncovered a roughly circular, horseshoe-shaped ditch with a central pit interpreted as the foundation for a wooden idol or post, surrounded by evidence of fire pits — a layout that does not match a Christian church and that most archaeologists read as a pre-Christian open-air sanctuary, consistent with the general East Slavic pattern (unlike the West Slavic Baltic coast) of worshipping without enclosed temple buildings.

## Chronicle connection

The name Peryn is transparently linked to Perun, and the *First Novgorod Chronicle* records that in 989, following Vladimir's conversion of Kiev the year before, the newly appointed bishop Akim (Joachim) had Novgorod's Perun idol thrown into the Volkhov, an episode local place-name tradition and the excavated site are usually connected to, though the chronicle's own wording does not name Peryn specifically — the identification rests on the site's location, layout, and name rather than an explicit textual statement placing the idol there.

primarySources.text: And Bishop Akim came to Novgorod, and destroyed the idols, and threw Perun into the Volkhov.
primarySources.date: entry for 989 CE; earliest surviving redaction (Synodal copy) 13th–14th c.

name: Onondaga Lake
description: The lake near present-day Syracuse, New York, where, in the account the Onondaga Nation and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy publish today, the Peacemaker and Hiawatha united the warring nations and planted the Great Tree of Peace.
detailedBio:
## The Confederacy's own account of its founding site

Onondaga Lake is named by the Onondaga Nation and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, on their own websites, as the place where the Great Law of Peace was founded: where the Peacemaker and Hiawatha persuaded the feared Onondaga leader Tadodaho to accept peace, and where the united nations planted the Great Tree of Peace. The Onondaga Nation's territory sits along the lake's southern end today, and the lake remains central to Haudenosaunee identity and to the Onondaga Nation's own environmental restoration efforts, work explicitly connected to caring for the site the Confederacy names as its birthplace.

## A living connection, not only a historical marker

This site follows the Onondaga Nation's and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy's own framing: Onondaga Lake is treated as a place of ongoing significance to a living political and cultural institution, the Confederacy's Grand Council still meets at Onondaga, not only as the site of a past event.

primarySources.text: Onondaga Lake is named as the site of the confederacy's founding, where the nations united in peace and planted the Great Tree of Peace.
The Onondaga Nation's own account of the council at Onondaga Lake that established the Great Law of Peace.

name: Haida Gwaii
description: The archipelago off the coast of British Columbia, formerly called the Queen Charlotte Islands, that is the Haida nation's homeland, and the setting of the story of Raven and the clamshell of the first people at Rose Spit.
detailedBio:
## Homeland and setting

Haida Gwaii is the Haida nation's home archipelago, and archaeological evidence, including finds in the islands' karst caves, documents human presence there for at least 10,000 to 13,000 years, among the longest continuously documented human occupations on the Northwest Coast. In Haida oral tradition, recorded by John R. Swanton and retold by the sculptor Bill Reid, it is also the setting of Raven's discovery of the giant clamshell at Rose Spit (Naikoon), from which he coaxes the first Haida people into the world.

## A living homeland

Haida Gwaii is not only the setting of a story from the past: it remains the Haida Nation's home today, governed in significant part through the Haida Nation's own institutions, and Haida artists and tellers continue to tell and depict the Raven stories associated with these islands.

primarySources.text: A Haida telling, from Charles Edenshaw of Masset and printed by Swanton as a supplementary text, of Raven finding the cockleshell of the first people on the beach at Haida Gwaii (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, Skidegate Dialect

name: The Sky World
description: The world above the sky in Haudenosaunee cosmology, with its people, lodges, and a great light-giving tree, from which Sky Woman fell through the hole left when the tree was uprooted.
detailedBio:
## The world before this one

Haudenosaunee cosmology begins not with emptiness but with another world: a Sky World above, where beings lived much as people do, in lodges, under a chief. At its centre stood a great tree whose blossoms gave light. When the tree was uprooted, whether because the chief dreamed it must be, or out of jealousy, or for reasons tellers give differently, a hole opened, and Sky Woman fell through it to the waters below.

## After the fall

The Sky World does not disappear from the story. In Parker's Seneca material Sapling visits his father there, and in several tellings Sky Woman returns to it. It is, in a sense, the model of which the earth is a copy, and the place from which the seeds of the first plants came.

primarySources.text: Parker summarises the Sky World, its chief, the great celestial tree, and its uprooting before Sky Woman's fall (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: Hewitt's texts describe the Sky World and its tree in differing detail in the Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk versions (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: J.N.B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43

name: Cohoes Falls
description: The great falls on the Mohawk River near its meeting with the Hudson, where, in the account the Onondaga Nation publishes, the Mohawk tested the Peacemaker by felling the tree he stood in over the water.
coordinateNote: The Onondaga Nation's account names Cohoes Falls as the place of the test; older written versions describe a falls on the Mohawk River without naming it.
detailedBio:
## The test

When the Peacemaker brought his message to the Mohawk, the easternmost of the five nations, they tested him. In the account the Onondaga Nation shares publicly, they had him climb a tree that overhung a great waterfall, now called Cohoes Falls, and then cut the tree down, so that he fell into the water. The next morning he was found alive, sitting by a fire, and the Mohawk accepted the Great Peace, becoming the first nation to do so.

## The place today

The falls, about 27 metres high, lie on the Mohawk River in the city of Cohoes, New York, just above its confluence with the Hudson. The site is honoured by Haudenosaunee people as the place where the message of peace was first accepted by a nation.

primarySources.text: The Mohawks instructed the Peacemaker to climb a tree overhanging a large waterfall, now named Cohoes Falls, and cut it down beneath him; he survived, and they accepted the message (paraphrase).

name: Nass River
description: The river of northern British Columbia at whose head, in the Tlingit Raven cycle, the wealthy old man kept the stars, moon, and sun in boxes; it is also one of the rivers Raven made from Petrel's stolen water.
coordinateNote: Pinned near the Nass estuary; the stories place the old man's house at the head of the river, which tellers do not locate precisely. The Nass is the homeland of the Nisga'a Nation.
detailedBio:
## At the head of the Nass

In the Tlingit Raven cycle, the wealthy old man who owns the stars, the moon, and daylight lives at the head of the Nass River, and his title, Naas Shaak Aankáawu, means 'Nobleman at the Head of the Nass'. The river was the centre of the eulachon (candlefish) fishery that drew Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, and Nisga'a traders every spring, a fitting place for the richest man in the world to live.

## Made by Raven

In the same Sitka cycle, the Nass is the first of the rivers Raven makes when he spits out the water stolen from Petrel. The river itself is the homeland of the Nisga'a Nation, whose own traditions of the Nass and of Raven (Txeemsim) are separate from the Tlingit stories told about it.

primarySources.text: Raven spits out Petrel's water to make the Nass and other rivers; the owner of daylight lives at the head of the Nass (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 39), "Raven" (Sitka, recorded in English)

name: Templo Mayor
description: The great twin temple at the heart of Tenochtitlan, dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, built as an image of the mountain Coatepec where Huitzilopochtli was born; excavated since 1978 in the centre of Mexico City.
detailedBio:
## Two shrines on one pyramid

The Huey Teocalli, the Templo Mayor, stood at the centre of the Mexica capital. Its double stairway led to two shrines: on the south side Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and on the north Tlaloc, god of rain, the two powers on which the city depended. The temple was enlarged at least seven times between the 14th century and its destruction by the Spanish in 1521.

## Coatepec made visible

The Huitzilopochtli side re-created the myth of his birth on Coatepec, Serpent Mountain, told in Book 3 of the *Florentine Codex*: born fully armed, he killed his sister Coyolxauhqui and threw her body down the mountain, where it broke apart. In 1978 electrical workers uncovered the great stone disc showing Coyolxauhqui dismembered at the foot of the stairs, exactly where the myth places her, and the discovery began the modern excavation.

## Today

The Museo del Templo Mayor beside the ruins holds the finds, including the Tlaltecuhtli monolith discovered in 2006.

primarySources.text: Huitzilopochtli is born on Coatepec, kills Coyolxauhqui, and casts her down the mountain, where her body breaks apart (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 3

primarySources.text: Excavation reports of the Proyecto Templo Mayor, begun after the 1978 discovery of the Coyolxauhqui stone (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, The Great Temple of the Aztecs

name: Omeyocan
description: The 'place of duality', the highest of the thirteen heavens in Nahua cosmology, home of the creator pair Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl (Ometeotl), from which the souls of children were said to descend.
detailedBio:
## The top of the heavens

Nahua sources describe the heavens as a series of levels, most often thirteen, above the earth. At the top is Omeyocan, 'the place of two' or 'place of duality', where the creator pair dwell: Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl, Lord and Lady of Duality, also called Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl. The *Florentine Codex* records speeches in which a newborn child is said to have been sent from that highest place.

## Sources and variation

The layered heavens are drawn and glossed in the *Codex Vaticanus A* (Codex Ríos), and the creator pair's role opens the *Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas*. The number and names of the heavens differ between sources, and some scholars argue the neat thirteen-level scheme owes something to its Spanish-era presentation. The idea of a dual creator at the top of the cosmos, however, runs through Nahua poetry and prayer.

primarySources.text: The highest heaven is the place of duality, home of the Lord and Lady of Duality, from which children are sent to be born (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 6

primarySources.text: The creator pair Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl dwell in the highest heaven and are the parents of the four Tezcatlipocas (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

name: Temple of Vesta
description: The small round temple in the Roman Forum where the Vestal Virgins kept the eternal fire of the state burning and guarded sacred objects, among them, tradition said, the Palladium brought from Troy.
detailedBio:
## The hearth of Rome

The Aedes Vestae was not a temple in the strict sense but a round shrine, recalling, the Romans said, the round huts of early Rome. Inside burned the fire of Vesta, the hearth of the whole city, tended day and night by the six Vestal Virgins. If it went out, the Vestal responsible was flogged and the fire rekindled by an ancient method. There was no cult statue; Ovid, in the *Fasti* (Book 6), says that Vesta is nothing other than living flame.

## The storeroom

An inner space, the penus, held sacred objects that only the Vestals could see. Among them, according to tradition reported by Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others, was the Palladium, the image of Pallas that Aeneas was said to have rescued from Troy. When the Gauls sacked Rome around 390 BCE, Livy says, the Vestals carried the sacred objects away to safety at Caere.

## The ruins

The shrine burned and was rebuilt several times; the partial reconstruction seen today in the Forum dates to the rebuilding after a fire in 191 CE under Julia Domna, restored in the 1930s. The House of the Vestals stands beside it. The fire was extinguished and the order disbanded under Theodosius I at the end of the 4th century.

primarySources.text: Ovid explains the round shape of Vesta's shrine and says that Vesta is nothing but living flame, which is why she has no image (paraphrase).
During the Gallic sack the Vestals carry the sacred objects out of the city to Caere (paraphrase).

name: Lake Nemi
description: The volcanic crater lake in the Alban Hills called Diana's Mirror, beside the sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis, whose priest, the rex Nemorensis, won his office by killing his predecessor.
detailedBio:
## Diana of the grove

On the north shore of the small crater lake near Aricia stood the sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis, 'Diana of the woodland', a cult shared by the Latin towns and later famous across the Roman world. The lake was called Speculum Dianae, Diana's Mirror. Women whose prayers were answered came in procession by torchlight, a scene Ovid mentions in the *Fasti*.

## The king of the grove

Ancient writers, among them Strabo (5.3.12) and Suetonius (*Caligula* 35), describe the strange rule of the priesthood: the priest, called the rex Nemorensis, was a runaway slave who won the office by killing the man who held it, and so lived always on guard, sword in hand. Strabo connects the custom with the Scythian cult of Artemis.

## Frazer's golden bough

James George Frazer opened *The Golden Bough* (1890) with this priesthood and linked it to the golden bough of Virgil's *Aeneid* Book 6, building a sweeping theory of dying and reviving kings. The link between Nemi and Virgil's bough is Frazer's own, drawn from a remark by the late-antique commentator Servius, and his theory is not accepted today.

## The ships

Two enormous ceremonial ships built under Caligula were raised from the lake in 1928 to 1932 and destroyed by fire in 1944.

primarySources.text: The priest of the Arician grove is a runaway slave who has killed his predecessor and goes always armed against the next challenger (paraphrase).
Caligula, jealous of the priest of Nemi's long tenure, hired a stronger man to challenge him (paraphrase).

name: Lake Avernus
description: The crater lake near Cumae in Campania that Roman poets placed at the entrance to the underworld; in the Aeneid, the Sibyl leads Aeneas down to the dead through the cave beside it.
detailedBio:
## The gate of the underworld

Avernus lies in the volcanic Phlegraean Fields west of Naples, close to the Greek colony of Cumae, home of the Sibyl. Its steep wooded crater and the sulphurous air of the area made it, for Greek and Roman writers, a natural entrance to the realm of the dead. In Book 6 of Virgil's *Aeneid*, Aeneas consults the Sibyl at Cumae, finds the golden bough, and descends with her through a deep cave by the dark lake, where no bird could fly over safely; the poem derives the name from the Greek aornos, 'birdless'.

## A real lake, a working harbour

The myth did not stop practical use. In 37 BCE Agrippa connected Avernus to the Lucrine Lake and the sea to create the naval base Portus Julius, and the tunnel called the Grotta di Cocceio was cut toward Cumae. Visitors in later centuries were shown a tunnel on the shore as the 'Sibyl's cave'.

## Proverbial

The Sibyl's warning that the descent to Avernus is easy, but the return is the real labour, became proverbial in Latin literature.

primarySources.text: Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, enters the underworld through a deep cave beside the dark lake over which birds cannot fly; the descent is easy, the return the labour (paraphrase).

name: Palatine Hill and the Lupercal
description: The hill where Romulus founded his city, with the Lupercal cave at its foot where tradition said the she-wolf nursed Romulus and Remus, and where the Lupercalia began each February.
detailedBio:
## Romulus's hill

In Livy's account (Book 1), the twins Romulus and Remus, exposed by order of the usurping king Amulius, are washed ashore at the foot of the Palatine, where a she-wolf finds and nurses them in a cave, the Lupercal. Grown, they quarrel over where to found their city; Romulus takes the auspices from the Palatine, fortifies it, and kills Remus when he leaps over the new wall. Rome's oldest traditions of kingship cling to the hill, and a hut said to be Romulus's own was preserved and repaired there into imperial times.

## The Lupercalia

On 15 February the Luperci, young men in goatskins, ran from the Lupercal around the Palatine, striking those they met with thongs of hide, a rite believed to bring fertility. Ovid explains it in the *Fasti* (Book 2), and Mark Antony famously offered Caesar a crown while running as a Lupercus in 44 BCE.

## House of emperors

Augustus chose to live on the Palatine beside Romulus's hut and the temple of Apollo, and later emperors built their palaces there, which is why the word palace comes from its name. A decorated underground chamber found in 2007 was proposed as the Lupercal; that identification is disputed.

primarySources.text: The exposed twins are nursed by a she-wolf at the foot of the Palatine; Romulus fortifies the Palatine and kills Remus when he leaps the wall (paraphrase).
Ovid explains the origins of the Lupercalia and the running of the Luperci (paraphrase).

name: Emain Macha
description: Navan Fort in County Armagh, the royal seat of Ulster in the Ulster Cycle, where King Conchobar held court and where Macha, forced to race while pregnant, cursed the men of Ulster.
detailedBio:
## The seat of the Ulaid

In the tales of the Ulster Cycle, Emain Macha is the court of Conchobar mac Nessa, home of the Red Branch warriors and the place from which the young Cú Chulainn sets out. Its name is explained in more than one way: as 'the twins of Macha', from the story of Macha's race, or from a Macha who marked out the fort with her brooch.

## Macha's curse

In the tale *Noínden Ulad* ('The Debility of the Ulstermen'), Macha, a woman of the otherworld, lives with a farmer who boasts at the king's assembly that his wife can outrun the king's horses. Though she is heavily pregnant, she is made to race; she wins, gives birth to twins at the finish, and curses the men of Ulster to suffer the pains of childbirth for days in their time of greatest need. That curse explains why, in the *Táin Bó Cúailnge*, the Ulstermen lie helpless as Medb's army invades, and only Cú Chulainn can defend the province.

## The archaeology

Navan Fort is a large ringed enclosure on a drumlin west of Armagh. Excavations found a remarkable structure of about 95 CE: a circular building of rings of posts, filled with stones, then deliberately burned and covered with a mound, apparently a ritual act. A Barbary ape skull from the site shows long-distance contacts. The site was a royal and ritual centre long before the tales were written down, but it cannot be tied to any individual in them.

primarySources.text: Macha is forced to race the king's horses while pregnant, bears twins at the finish, and curses the men of Ulster with the debility of childbirth (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Noínden Ulad (The Debility of the Ulstermen), preserved in the Book of Leinster

primarySources.text: The Ulstermen are laid low by their debility while Medb's army invades, and Cú Chulainn alone holds the border (paraphrase).

name: Rathcroghan (Cruachan)
description: The royal complex of Connacht in County Roscommon, seat of Queen Medb and King Ailill in the Táin, whose cave Oweynagat was said to be a door to the otherworld.
detailedBio:
## Medb's court

Cruachan is the court of Medb and Ailill, queen and king of Connacht, in the Ulster Cycle. The *Táin Bó Cúailnge* in its later recension opens here with their pillow-talk: comparing their possessions, they find them equal except that Ailill owns the great bull Finnbennach, and Medb resolves to take the Brown Bull of Cooley from Ulster to match it. The war of the Táin begins at Cruachan and its bulls finally fight across Ireland.

## The cave of the cats

Oweynagat, 'the cave of the cats', a natural cave entered through a souterrain, was known in medieval tradition as an entrance to the otherworld. In *Echtra Nerai* ('The Adventure of Nera') a man of Ailill's court enters the síd of Cruachan at Samhain, and other tales bring monstrous creatures and the Morrígan out of it.

## The landscape

Rathcroghan is a spread of more than 200 archaeological sites, mounds, enclosures, and linear earthworks, spanning thousands of years. It is interpreted by the Rathcroghan Visitor Centre at Tulsk; like Emain Macha and Tara, it was a real royal centre that the tales remember in their own way.

primarySources.text: At Cruachan, Medb and Ailill compare their wealth, and Medb resolves to take the Brown Bull of Cooley to equal Ailill's bull (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Táin Bó Cúailnge (Book of Leinster recension)

primarySources.text: Nera enters the otherworld mound of Cruachan on Samhain night (paraphrase).
primarySources.date: Old or Middle Irish tale; manuscripts 14th century

name: Aquae Sulis (Bath)
description: The hot springs at Bath in southwest England, sacred to the British goddess Sulis, whom the Romans identified with Minerva; worshippers cast curse tablets into the sacred spring asking her to punish thieves.
detailedBio:
## Sulis Minerva

The only natural hot springs in Britain rise at Bath. The Romans built a temple and bathing complex here from the later 1st century CE and called the town Aquae Sulis, 'the waters of Sulis', keeping the name of the local goddess. In inscriptions she is Sulis or Sulis Minerva, the British deity paired with the Roman goddess of wisdom. The gilded bronze head of the cult statue survives, as does the temple pediment with its striking moustached Gorgon-like head.

## Curses in the spring

More than 130 curse tablets (defixiones), sheets of lead or pewter inscribed and thrown into the sacred spring, have been recovered. Most ask Sulis to punish the thief of a cloak, gloves, or coins, often naming suspects and demanding that the culprit suffer until the goods are returned to the temple. They are among the most direct evidence for the everyday religion of Roman Britain, and some include a few words that may be British Celtic.

## A perpetual fire

The 3rd-century writer Solinus describes Minerva's temple at the hot springs, where the fire on her altar never went out and burned not to ash but to stony lumps, probably a reference to coal.

primarySources.text: Lead curse tablets from the sacred spring petition Sulis to punish thieves of cloaks, rings, and coins (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: R. S. O. Tomlin, Tabellae Sulis: Roman Inscribed Tablets of Tin and Lead from the Sacred Spring at Bath

primarySources.text: At the hot springs in Britain, Minerva's temple has a perpetual fire that turns not to ash but to stony masses (paraphrase).

name: Mag Tuired (Moytirra)
description: The plain in County Sligo identified with the second Battle of Mag Tuired, where, in Irish mythic history, the Túatha Dé Danann defeated the Fomorians and Lug killed Balor with a sling-stone.
coordinateNote: The medieval texts place the first battle near Cong in County Mayo and the second near Lough Arrow in County Sligo; the Sligo townland of Moytirra preserves the name, but no battle is historically attested.
detailedBio:
## Two battles

Irish mythic history, as told in the *Lebor Gabála Érenn* and in the tale *Cath Maige Tuired*, describes two battles on plains called Mag Tuired, 'the plain of towers' or 'of pillars'. In the first, the Túatha Dé Danann defeat the Fir Bolg, and their king Núadu loses his arm. In the second, they fight the Fomorians under the tyranny of Bres.

## The second battle

*Cath Maige Tuired*, preserved in a 16th-century manuscript of an older text, tells how Lug, master of every art, organises the Túatha Dé for war; Dian Cécht's healing well restores the wounded each night and Goibniu's forge replaces broken weapons. In the battle Balor of the baleful eye, whose gaze destroys armies, is killed by Lug's sling-stone, which drives the eye through the back of his head against his own host. The Morrígan's prophecy closes the tale.

## On the map

The second battle was placed near Lough Arrow in County Sligo, where the townland of Moytirra and a landscape of cairns and megalithic tombs keep the name. The identification is medieval learned tradition attached to an ancient ritual landscape, not a record of a real battle.

primarySources.text: The Túatha Dé Danann defeat the Fomorians at the second battle of Mag Tuired; Lug kills Balor with a sling-stone through his eye (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired)

name: Hattusa
description: The Hittite capital near modern Boğazkale in central Türkiye, whose temple archives preserved almost every Hittite myth known today.
detailedBio:
## Capital and archive

Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite kingdom for most of its history, from the reign of Hattusili I in the seventeenth century BCE until the city was abandoned around 1180 BCE. Its ruins, near the village of Boğazkale (formerly Boğazköy) in Çorum Province, include massive fortification walls, gates carved with lions and sphinxes, and dozens of temples. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

## Where the myths were found

German excavations beginning in 1906 recovered tens of thousands of clay tablet fragments from the temples and palace archives. Among them were treaties, prayers, festival texts, and the mythological texts on this site: the Illuyanka tales, the Disappearance of Telipinu, and the Hittite translations of the Hurrian Kumarbi cycle. It was on the basis of these tablets that Bedřich Hrozný identified Hittite as an Indo-European language in 1915.

## The Great Temple

The largest temple in the lower city, often called Temple 1, is generally thought to have been dedicated to the Storm-god of Hatti and the Sun-goddess of Arinna, the two chief deities of the state. Its storerooms held large numbers of tablets and storage vessels.

primarySources.text: The mythological tablets of CTH 321, 324, and 344-348 were excavated in the archives of Hattusa and published in the series Keilschrifttexte aus Boghazköi (KBo) and Keilschrifturkunden aus Boghazköi (KUB).
primarySources.source: H. A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths (introduction and text notes)

name: Yazılıkaya
description: An open-air rock sanctuary just outside Hattusa whose carved procession of gods and goddesses, labelled in Hieroglyphic Luwian, shows the Hurrian-influenced pantheon of the thirteenth century BCE.
detailedBio:
## A gallery of the gods

Yazılıkaya ("inscribed rock" in Turkish) is a natural rock sanctuary about a kilometre and a half northeast of Hattusa. In its main chamber, reliefs carved mostly in the thirteenth century BCE show two processions converging on the back wall: gods on the left and goddesses on the right, each labelled with a name in Hieroglyphic Luwian.

## The meeting of Teššub and Hebat

At the centre, the storm-god Teššub, standing on two mountain-gods, faces the goddess Hebat, who stands on a panther; behind her comes their son Šarruma. The names are Hurrian, reflecting the Hurrian theology promoted by the royal family in the thirteenth century, and the procession is often compared with the Hurrian offering lists (kaluti) that rank gods in the same order. Šauška appears on both sides of the procession.

## King Tudhaliya IV

A large relief shows King Tudhaliya IV, who is usually credited with the sanctuary's final form, and a smaller chamber holds a relief of Šarruma embracing the king, along with the enigmatic "sword god". The sanctuary may have been used for the spring festival; its exact function is still debated.

primarySources.text: The Hieroglyphic Luwian labels of the main chamber name the gods of the procession, headed by Teššub and Hebat, in an order close to Hurrian offering lists.
primarySources.source: E. Laroche, 'Le panthéon de Yazılıkaya', Journal of Cuneiform Studies 6

name: Nerik (Oymaağaç Höyük)
description: The holy city of the Storm-god of Nerik in the north of the Hittite lands, where the Illuyanka story was recited at the Purulli festival; identified with Oymaağaç Höyük near Vezirköprü.
detailedBio:
## The Storm-god's northern city

Nerik was one of the oldest and holiest cult centres of the Hattian and Hittite world, the seat of the Storm-god of Nerik, who was regarded as a son of the Storm-god of Hatti. The Illuyanka tales present themselves as the words of Kella, a priest of the Storm-god of Nerik, and link the serpent myth to the Purulli festival celebrated there.

## Lost and restored

For much of the Hittite period Nerik lay in territory overrun by the Kaška, a people of the Black Sea hinterland, and the Hittite kings could not reach it; its cult was maintained from other towns. Hattusili III, in the thirteenth century BCE, recovered and rebuilt the city and made much of its restoration in his own texts.

## Oymaağaç Höyük

Since 2005 a German-Turkish excavation at Oymaağaç Höyük, in the Vezirköprü district of Samsun Province, has uncovered a large Hittite temple and cuneiform tablets mentioning Nerik, and the site is now widely identified as the ancient city. The coordinates given here are those of the mound.

primarySources.text: The Illuyanka text introduces itself as the words of Kella, priest of the Storm-god of Nerik, concerning the Purulli festival (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Illuyanka tales, CTH 321, trans. H. A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths

name: Urkeš (Tell Mozan)
description: The ancient Hurrian city in northeastern Syria that the Kumarbi cycle names as Kumarbi's home, identified with the mound of Tell Mozan.
detailedBio:
## Kumarbi's city

In the Hurrian songs preserved at Hattusa, Kumarbi is the god of Urkeš: in the Song of Ullikummi he takes counsel in his mind and sets out from his city of Urkeš to plan Teššub's downfall. Hurrian tradition regarded Urkeš as an ancient and venerable city, and a Hurrian foundation inscription of its early kings has been found.

## Tell Mozan

Excavations at Tell Mozan in northeastern Syria, directed by Giorgio Buccellati and Marilyn Kelly-Buccellati from 1984, identified the site as Urkeš through inscribed seal impressions naming its kings (endan). Finds include a large temple terrace and a deep underground stone structure that the excavators interpret as a ritual pit (ābi) for communicating with the underworld, the kind of pit Hurrian rituals used to call up the Former Gods.

## Not a Hittite city

Urkeš was never part of the Hittite kingdom; it belongs on this site because the Hurrian myths the Hittites translated place Kumarbi there. It is a reminder that the Kumarbi cycle comes from a different world from native Anatolian tradition.

primarySources.text: Kumarbi takes wisdom into his mind and rises from his city Urkeš to plan a rival for Teššub (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Song of Ullikummi, CTH 345, trans. H. A. Hoffner Jr., Hittite Myths

name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)
description: The Late Bronze Age port city on the Syrian coast whose archives of alphabetic cuneiform tablets preserve the Baal Cycle and the epics of Aqhat and Kirta; destroyed around 1185 BCE.
detailedBio:
## Discovery

In 1928 a farmer ploughing near the bay of Minet el-Beida, north of Latakia, broke into an ancient tomb. The following year French excavators under Claude Schaeffer began digging at the nearby mound of Ras Shamra and found the city of Ugarit, known from Egyptian and Hittite records but until then unlocated. Excavation has continued, with interruptions, ever since.

## A cosmopolitan port

Ugarit was a wealthy kingdom trading with Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean, the Hittite empire (to which it was a vassal), and Mesopotamia. Its scribes wrote in Akkadian, Sumerian, Hurrian, Hittite, Egyptian, Cypro-Minoan, and in their own Ugaritic language, for which they used an alphabet of thirty cuneiform signs. Multilingual god-lists from the site equate the Ugaritic gods with Hurrian and Mesopotamian ones.

## Temples and archives

Two temples on the acropolis are generally identified as those of Baal and of Dagan. The mythological tablets were found mostly in the house of the high priest nearby, and several carry the colophon of the scribe Ilimilku. The city was destroyed around 1185 BCE during the upheavals that ended the Late Bronze Age, and never reoccupied as a city.

primarySources.text: Colophon: the scribe Ilimilku, student of the chief priest, wrote the tablet in the reign of Niqmaddu, king of Ugarit (paraphrase).
primarySources.date: tablets of the late 13th or early 12th c. BCE

name: Mount Zaphon (Jebel Aqra)
description: The mountain north of Ugarit, now Jebel Aqra on the Syrian-Turkish border, where Baal's palace stands in myth; the Hurrian-Hittite Mount Hazzi and the Greek Mount Kasios.
detailedBio:
## Baal's mountain

Ṣapānu, Zaphon, is Baal's home in the Ugaritic texts. His palace is built on its heights, Anat buries his body there, and he and Mot fight their final battle on it. Baal is often called Baal of Zaphon, and Ugaritic ritual texts treat the mountain itself as divine, listing offerings to it.

## A real mountain

Zaphon is Jebel Aqra (Kel Dağı in Turkish), rising about 1,700 metres from the coast at the mouth of the Orontes, some 40 kilometres north of Ugarit and visible from the city. Storms build over it from the sea, which suits a storm-god's seat.

## One mountain, many gods

The same mountain was Mount Hazzi to the Hurrians and Hittites, where the storm-god Teššub climbs to look at the stone giant Ullikummi, and Mount Kasios to the Greeks, where Zeus Kasios was worshipped and where some Greek sources place Zeus's battle with Typhon. The Hebrew word ṣāpôn, "north", derives from the mountain's name, and Psalm 48 describes Mount Zion as "the heights of Zaphon". Few places in the ancient world show so clearly how one sacred landscape passed between traditions.

primarySources.text: Anat carries Baal's body to the heights of Zaphon, weeps, and buries him there (paraphrase).
primarySources.date: tablets of the late 13th or early 12th c. BCE

coordinateNote: Baal's mountain Zaphon is identified with Jebel Aqra (Mount Kasios) on the Syrian–Turkish coast north of Ugarit.

name: The Source of the Two Rivers
description: El's remote dwelling 'at the source of the two rivers, in the midst of the springs of the two deeps', where gods and messengers go to seek his decisions; a mythical place without a known earthly location.
detailedBio:
## Where El lives

Whenever a god in the Baal Cycle needs El's decision, the text uses a set formula: the traveller sets face toward El, at the source of the two rivers, in the midst of the springs of the two deeps, enters his domain, and comes to the pavilion of the King, the Father of Years (paraphrase). The dwelling is a tent or pavilion rather than a palace, and it lies at the far edge of the world, where the waters of the deep rise.

## The mountain of assembly

A related place is the mountain where the assembly of the gods meets, which Ugaritic texts call Mount Lel (or the mountain of Night); Yam's messengers come to the gods feasting there in KTU 1.2 I. Whether the source of the rivers and the mountain of assembly are the same place is not clear.

## Not on the map

Scholars have tried to identify El's home with real places, including sources of the Jordan or springs in Lebanon, but the texts give no geography, and this site treats it as a mythical realm. The idea of a god dwelling where the cosmic waters rise has a parallel in the Mesopotamian Enki's home in the Apsu, and some interpreters compare the biblical Eden's rivers.

primarySources.text: She sets her face toward El at the source of the two rivers, in the midst of the springs of the two deeps; she enters the domain of El and comes to the pavilion of the King, Father of Years (paraphrase).
primarySources.date: tablets of the late 13th or early 12th c. BCE

name: Cumberland Sound (Kangiqtualuk)
description: The deep inlet on the east coast of Baffin Island, Nunavut, where Franz Boas recorded the story of Sedna and her father Anguta in 1883-84; home of the community of Pangnirtung.
detailedBio:
## Where 'Sedna' was written down

Franz Boas spent the winter of 1883-84 among the Inuit of Cumberland Sound, based largely at the whaling station on Kekerten Island. His ethnography *The Central Eskimo* (1888), drawing on what people there told him, includes the account of Sedna, her fulmar husband, and her father Anguta that made "Sedna" the name by which the Sea Woman is best known outside the Arctic. The coordinates given here mark the approximate centre of the sound.

## A whaling world

In Boas's time Cumberland Sound was a centre of the Scottish and American whaling trade, and Inuit worked closely with the whalers; Kekerten is now a territorial historic park. Boas also recorded the autumn feasts associated with Sedna that were held in the sound's camps.

## Pangnirtung today

The community of Pangnirtung (Panniqtuuq), on the sound's northeast shore, is known for its print shop and weaving studio, whose artists have depicted the Sea Woman among many other subjects. The story Boas recorded here continues to be told and interpreted by Inuit artists of the region.

primarySources.text: Boas describes great autumn feasts in the Cumberland Sound camps connected with the Sedna tradition (paraphrase).

name: Igloolik (Iglulik)
description: The island community in the Foxe Basin, Nunavut, whose people told Knud Rasmussen about the Sea Woman, the Moon Spirit, and Sila in the 1920s, and whose elders continue to share that knowledge.
detailedBio:
## Aua's country

In 1922 Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition stayed among the Iglulingmiut, and the angakkuq Aua and his family became among his most important teachers. *Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos* (1929) records their accounts of Takanaaluk, the Sea Woman; of Taqqiq, the Moon Spirit; and of Sila, as well as Aua's often-quoted explanation that people observe their rules not because they know why, but because they fear what happens when they are broken.

## An archaeological heartland

The Igloolik area is rich in archaeological sites from the Dorset and Thule periods, the ancestors of today's Inuit and the earlier people Inuit tradition calls the Tuniit.

## Keeping knowledge

Igloolik has been a centre of Inuit-led cultural work. The Igloolik Oral History Project has recorded elders' knowledge for decades, and the film company Isuma, founded there, made *Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner* (2001), the first feature film written, directed, and acted in Inuktitut, which retells an Iglulik legend.

primarySources.text: Iglulik speakers, among them Aua, describe to Rasmussen the Sea Spirit, the Moon Spirit, and Sila (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Knud Rasmussen, Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos (Report of the Fifth Thule Expedition 1921-24, vol. 7, no. 1)

name: Tikiġaq (Point Hope)
description: The Iñupiaq whaling village on a gravel spit in the Chukchi Sea, northwest Alaska, whose land, in the community's tradition, is the body of a sea creature harpooned by Raven Man.
detailedBio:
## An ancient whaling point

Tikiġaq, whose name refers to its shape as a pointing finger, stands on a long spit extending into the Chukchi Sea. People have lived here for well over a thousand years; the nearby site of Ipiutak, excavated around 1940, revealed an extraordinary early Arctic culture, and the village's later history is bound up with the hunting of bowhead whales from the ice edge each spring.

## The land as a whale

In Tikiġaq tradition, as told by elders to Tom Lowenstein and published in *Ancient Land: Sacred Whale* (1993), the land of the point was once a great creature of the sea, harpooned by Tulunigraq, Raven Man; its body became the land on which the village stands. The story ties the community's home to the hunt that sustains it.

## Today

Point Hope remains an active Iñupiaq whaling community in the North Slope Borough of Alaska. Coastal erosion has forced the village to move inland from its old site, and the community, like others in the Arctic, faces rapid environmental change.

primarySources.text: Tikiġaq elders describe the point as the body of the creature harpooned by Raven Man (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Tom Lowenstein, Ancient Land: Sacred Whale

name: Torngat Mountains
description: The mountains of northern Labrador and Nunavik whose name is usually explained as 'place of spirits', from the Inuktitut tuurngait; now a national park co-managed with the Inuit of Nunatsiavut and Nunavik.
detailedBio:
## Place of spirits

The Torngat Mountains rise along the northern tip of Labrador, on the boundary between Nunatsiavut (Labrador) and Nunavik (Quebec). Their name is usually explained as coming from tuurngait, the helping spirits of Inuit belief, so that it means something like "place of spirits"; Labrador traditions recorded in the early twentieth century associated the region with Torngarsoak, the great spirit. The coordinates given here mark the approximate centre of the range.

## A homeland

Inuit and their predecessors have used the Torngat coast for thousands of years, hunting, fishing, and travelling through its fjords. In the twentieth century many Inuit families were relocated away from the northern Labrador coast, and the return of Inuit to the land through park base camps and programmes has been an important part of cultural renewal.

## Co-management

Torngat Mountains National Park, created under the Labrador Inuit Land Claims Agreement (a park reserve from 2005 and a national park from 2008), is co-managed by Parks Canada and a board including Inuit of Nunatsiavut and Nunavik, and Inuit guides and bear guards work with visitors. It is an example of the land associated with spirits being cared for by the people whose tradition named it.

primarySources.text: Labrador Inuit traditions of Torngarsoak, the great spirit associated with the northern mountains (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: E. W. Hawkes, The Labrador Eskimo (Geological Survey of Canada, Memoir 91)

name: Baiame's Ngunnhu (Brewarrina Fish Traps)
description: Stone fish traps in the Barwon River at Brewarrina, New South Wales, whose design the ancestral creation being Baiame revealed; National Heritage listed in 2005 and cared for by the Ngemba people and their neighbours.
detailedBio:
## A system of stone

Baiame's Ngunnhu is a network of dry-stone walls and pens across the Barwon River at Brewarrina, in north-western New South Wales. The design guided fish, especially during spring migrations, into pens where they could be caught, and resisted both floods and low water. It is among the largest and most complex Aboriginal fish-trap systems known.

## Story and law

According to the Ngemba people and their neighbours, as recorded in the National Heritage listing, the ancestral creation being Baiame revealed the design by throwing his net over the river, built the traps with his two sons, and allocated them to family groups who were responsible for their use and maintenance. Neighbouring peoples gathered here for ceremony and trade.

## Heritage and care

The traps were damaged after colonisation, and a weir later built across the river altered its flow and buried part of them. They were added to the National Heritage List in 2005. The Brewarrina Aboriginal community continues to care for the traps, and the site is visited through local Aboriginal-led cultural tourism. The coordinates given here are approximate.

primarySources.text: The Ngemba people of Brewarrina used their advanced knowledge of river hydrology and fish ecology to trap and catch large numbers of fresh water fish.
primarySources.source: Australian Government, National Heritage List: Brewarrina Aboriginal Fish Traps (Baiame's Ngunnhu)

name: Bunjil's Shelter
description: A rock shelter in the Black Range near Stawell, Victoria, on Djab Wurrung Country, holding the only known rock painting of Bunjil.
detailedBio:
## Bunjil in the rock

Bunjil's Shelter, in the Black Range Scenic Reserve about ten kilometres south of Stawell in western Victoria, holds a painting of a figure understood as Bunjil, with two dogs, the only rock painting of Bunjil known. The site is on Djab Wurrung Country and is significant to the Djab Wurrung and other Kulin and neighbouring peoples; Bunjil is also said to have sheltered in the Gariwerd (Grampians) region.

## Protection

The painting is protected behind a grille, and the site is managed as a heritage place. Visitors are asked to treat it with respect. Research on the painting has considered its age and the way it has been retouched over time, but its meaning is for its custodians to explain.

## Part of a wider landscape

Bunjil's Shelter lies near Gariwerd, a region rich in rock art sites managed with Traditional Owners, and near the Brambuk cultural centre at Halls Gap, where Aboriginal communities of the region share aspects of their culture with visitors.

primarySources.text: Rock art research on Bunjil's Shelter in the Black Range near Stawell, in Djab Wurrung Country (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Rock Art Research, 'Bunyip, Bunjil and mother-in-law avoidance'

name: Derbarl Yerrigan (Swan River)
description: The river that runs through Perth, Western Australia, whose course Whadjuk Noongar tradition attributes to the Wagyl; its resting places, including Goonininup below Kaarta Gar-up (Kings Park), are important Noongar places.
detailedBio:
## A Noongar river

The Derbarl Yerrigan, the Swan River, flows from the Darling Scarp through Perth to the Indian Ocean at Fremantle. For Whadjuk Noongar people it is at the heart of Country: a source of food and fresh water and a place of story. In the public Noongar telling, the Wagyl shaped the river in the Nyitting as it moved across the land. The coordinates given here mark Perth Water, in the city.

## Goonininup

At the foot of Kaarta Gar-up (Mount Eliza, below Kings Park) is Goonininup, near a freshwater spring, associated with the Wagyl. From 1989 Noongar people protested the redevelopment of the Old Swan Brewery on this site; the protest became a landmark in Western Australian heritage politics.

## Today

Noongar names for the river and for places along it are increasingly used in Perth, and Noongar-led tours and public art along the foreshore share aspects of the Derbarl Yerrigan's story with residents and visitors.

primarySources.text: During the Nyitting (Creation Time), the great creator snake called the Waugal or Wagyl moved down the Derbal Yerrigan and created the waterways and landscapes.

name: Uluṟu
description: The great sandstone monolith in Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Northern Territory, shaped by the actions of Aṉangu ancestral beings, including Kuniya and the Liru; jointly managed by Aṉangu and Parks Australia.
detailedBio:
## Aṉangu Country

Uluṟu is part of the Country of the Aṉangu, the traditional owners of Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park. For Aṉangu, the features of Uluṟu are evidence of the actions of ancestral beings in the Tjukurpa: the Kuniya (woma python) and the Liru (venomous snake men), the Mala (rufous hare-wallaby) people, and others. Some of these stories are shared publicly with visitors; many are not.

## Handback and joint management

Title to Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa was handed back to its traditional owners on 26 October 1985, and the park has since been jointly managed by Aṉangu and Parks Australia. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for both its natural and cultural values.

## Respect

Aṉangu ask visitors not to photograph certain culturally sensitive areas. Climbing Uluṟu, long discouraged by the traditional owners, was permanently closed in October 2019. Visitors can learn the publicly shared stories along walks such as the Kuniya walk to Muṯitjulu Waterhole.

primarySources.text: Aṉangu share the Kuniya and Liru Tjukurpa publicly along the walk to Muṯitjulu Waterhole (paraphrase).
primarySources.source: Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park (Parks Australia, with Aṉangu traditional owners), 'The Kuniya & Liru stories'

name: Sisnaajiní (Blanca Peak)
description: The sacred mountain of the east bounding Diné Bikéyah, in the Sangre de Cristo Range of southern Colorado, associated with white shell and the dawn.
detailedBio:
## The eastern boundary

Sisnaajiní, known in English as Blanca Peak, is the sacred mountain of the east, one of the four that bound Diné Bikéyah. It rises to about 4,370 metres in the Sierra Blanca massif of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in southern Colorado. It is associated with the east, with the dawn, and with white shell.

## A holy mountain

In the Diné origin story the sacred mountains were set in place by the Holy People after the emergence, each with its own adornments and associations. Soil and other materials from the four mountains are used in ceremonies that this site does not describe.

## Today

The mountain lies outside the present boundaries of the Navajo Nation, on land that includes private and public holdings. Diné people continue to regard it as sacred, and the protection of the sacred mountains is a recurring concern of the Navajo Nation.

primarySources.text: The Holy People set the sacred mountains in place at the four directions after the emergence (paraphrase).

name: Tsoodził (Mount Taylor)
description: The sacred mountain of the south, in New Mexico, associated with turquoise; near it the Hero Twins killed Yéʼiitsoh, whose blood is said to have become the lava flows of the region.
detailedBio:
## The southern boundary

Tsoodził, known in English as Mount Taylor, is the sacred mountain of the south, a volcanic peak rising to about 3,445 metres near Grants, New Mexico. It is associated with the south and with turquoise, and it is sacred to several peoples of the region, including the Acoma and Laguna Pueblos, Zuni, and Hopi as well as the Diné.

## Yéʼiitsoh

In the Hero Twins' story, the giant Yéʼiitsoh lived near Tsoodził, and the twins killed him at a lake nearby. Widely told accounts say his blood became the black lava flows, the malpais, near the mountain, and his head became Cabezon Peak to the east.

## Protection

In 2008 and 2009 the State of New Mexico listed Mount Taylor as a Traditional Cultural Property at the request of Native nations, including the Navajo Nation, amid concern over proposed uranium mining; the listing was upheld by the New Mexico Supreme Court in 2014.

primarySources.text: The twins meet Yéitso at a lake near Tsoťsil and kill him with lightning (paraphrase).

name: Dookʼoʼoosłííd (San Francisco Peaks)
description: The sacred mountain of the west, near Flagstaff, Arizona, associated with abalone shell; sacred to many Native nations, and the subject of long legal disputes over a ski resort.
detailedBio:
## The western boundary

Dookʼoʼoosłííd, the San Francisco Peaks, is the sacred mountain of the west, whose highest summit, Humphreys Peak, reaches about 3,850 metres north of Flagstaff, Arizona. It is associated with the west and with abalone shell. The peaks are sacred to many Native nations of the region, including the Hopi, for whom they are the home of the katsinam, as well as the Diné.

## A contested mountain

The peaks have been the focus of long legal and political disputes over the Arizona Snowbowl ski resort, including its use of treated wastewater to make artificial snow, which the Navajo Nation, the Hopi Tribe, and others opposed as a desecration. In *Navajo Nation v. United States Forest Service* (2008), a federal appeals court ruled against the tribes. The dispute is often cited in discussions of sacred-site protection in the United States.

## In the story

Along with the other sacred mountains, Dookʼoʼoosłííd was set in place by the Holy People after the emergence, and it marks the western edge of Diné Bikéyah, toward which Changing Woman went to live.

primarySources.text: The Holy People set the sacred mountains in place at the four directions after the emergence (paraphrase).

name: Dibé Ntsaa (Hesperus Mountain)
description: The sacred mountain of the north, usually identified with Hesperus Mountain in the La Plata Mountains of southwestern Colorado, associated with jet.
detailedBio:
## The northern boundary

Dibé Ntsaa, "big mountain sheep", is the sacred mountain of the north, usually identified with Hesperus Mountain, the highest summit of the La Plata Mountains in southwestern Colorado, at about 4,035 metres. It is associated with the north and with jet (black stone).

## Identification

Most sources identify Dibé Ntsaa with Hesperus Mountain, but some Diné accounts and scholars have identified the northern sacred mountain differently, and this site notes that the identification is not uniform.

## In the story

With Sisnaajiní, Tsoodził, and Dookʼoʼoosłííd, Dibé Ntsaa bounds Diné Bikéyah, the land into which the people emerged and within which, in the Diné understanding, they belong.

primarySources.text: The Holy People set the sacred mountains in place at the four directions after the emergence (paraphrase).

name: Chʼóolʼį́ʼí (Gobernador Knob)
description: A small peak in the Dinétah region of northern New Mexico where, in many tellings, First Man found the infant Changing Woman.
detailedBio:
## Where Changing Woman was found

Chʼóolʼį́ʼí, known in English as Gobernador Knob, is a small summit in Rio Arriba County, northern New Mexico, within the Four Corners region. In many tellings of the Diné origin story, it is here that First Man, following the sound of a baby's cry beneath a dark cloud, found the infant who would become Changing Woman.

## Dinétah

Chʼóolʼį́ʼí lies in Dinétah, the region along the upper San Juan River where, in Diné tradition and in the archaeological record, early Diné life was centred. Together with nearby Dziłnaʼoodiłii (Huerfano Mountain), it is among the sacred mountains within the land bounded by the four directional mountains.

## Respect

The knob is on public land, and it remains a sacred place for Diné people. This site gives its location because it is widely published, and asks readers to treat it accordingly.
